projectDesc.p: This dictionary comes to you through nice people making it available for free and for good. It is part of the FreeDict project, http://www.freedict.org/. This project aims to make available many translating dictionaries for free. Your contributions are welcome!

revisionDesc.change: Change numbering scheme from YYYY-MM-DD to YYYY.MM.DD
Use ref tag to encode license URL

sense.def: Possessive marker, indicating that an object belongs to the noun or noun phrase bearing the marker.
In the absence of a specified object, used to indicate “the house/place/establishment of”.
(in verbs) to act in the specified manner
(added to certain adjectives and adverbs, now especially short ones) More; used to form the comparative.
(added to certain adverbs) More; used to form the comparative.
Used to form the superlative of adjectives and adverbs.
A substantive suffix denoting a condition or state of being.
To produce verbs meaning to make.
Used to form nouns denoting materials or systems of objects which are used or employed in an action, or considered collectively.
(of adjectives from numbers, especially of times and ages) About, approximately.
state of
Used to form an uncountable noun from an adjective; especially, to form the noun referring to the state, property, or quality of conforming to the adjective's description.
Used to form verbs from nouns or adjectives, especially similative verbs
Used to form the name of a territory, country, or region.
Lacking (something); without (something). Added usually to a noun to form an adjective signifying a lack of that noun.
A branch of learning; a study of a particular subject.
Used to form the names of measuring devices.
Appended to adjectives to form nouns meaning "the state of being (the adjective)", "the quality of being (the adjective)", or "the measure of being (the adjective)".
(often, humorous) added to an ordinary English word to create a name for a (possibly non-existent) field of study.
(anime and manga fandom) Appended to a person's name or nickname to convey honour and respect.
Used to form cardinal numbers from thirteen to nineteen.
(mathematics) Used to form a term denoting the ordinal numeral corresponding to the value, being a natural number, of a mathematical expression.
Added to nouns and adjectives to form adjectives meaning “having the quality of”, either “involving the referent” or “analogous to it”.
Forming abstract nouns denoting a condition, quality, or state.
(chiefly, US, often, postpositive) Basic, beginner, starting from scratch.
deux chevaux (conventional French shortening of deux chevaux-vapeur "two horsepower") (a model of car by French manufacturer, Citroën)
(music) The minor key with A as its tonic, consisting of the pitches A, B, C, D, E, F, and G.
(music) The minor chord with a root of A.
(slang) An atomic bomb; a weapon that derives its energy from nuclear reactions and has enormous destructive power.
(music) the minor key with A as its tonic
(obsolete) A primer for teaching the Latin alphabet and first elements of reading. [Attested from around (1350 to 1470) until the mid-17th century.]
The fundamentals of any subject. [First attested in the mid-16th century.]
(electricity) Initialism of alternating current (often used to indicate an alternating potential rather than a current).
(often, punctuated) Initialism of annō Dominī (borrowed from Latin); in the year of our Lord.
(artificial intelligence, economics) A period of reduced funding and interest in artificial intelligence research.
(disease, acronym) Acquired immune deficiency syndrome. [from 1982]
(logic) Alternative form of ∧, the conjunction operator.
(banking) Initialism of automated teller machine or initialism of automatic teller machine.
A city in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany.
A city and port in Denmark, in East Jutland; the second-largest city in Denmark.
A en given name.
(biblical character) The son of Adam and Eve who was killed by his brother Cain.
the de facto capital and largest city of Ivory Coast.
Abkhazian: of or pertaining to Abkhazia, the Abkhazian people, or their language.
An Abkhazian; a native or inhabitant of Abkhazia, a region just east of the Black Sea. [Mid 19th century.]
A Northwest Caucasian language spoken in Abkhazia. [Mid 19th century.]

A region and de-facto independent but largely unrecognized country on the coast of the Black Sea and the south-western flank of the Caucasus, which considers itself an independent state called the Republic of Abkhazia; considered part of Georgia's territory by the Georgian government and the vast majority of the international community.
(dated, now, offensive) An Aboriginal person from Australia (descending from, or a member of, one of the indigenous people(s) before British colonisation), Aboriginal Australian.

(Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Baha'i) A prophet in the Old Testament, Qur'an and Aqdas; a Semitic patriarch son of Terah who practiced monotheism, father of the Jewish patriarch Isaac by Sarah and the Arab patriarch Ishmael by Hagar. [First attested prior to 1150.]
A en given name. [First attested prior to 1150.]
A surname originating as a patronymic. [First attested prior to 1150.]
Abraham (prophet in the Old Testament). [First attested prior to 1150.]
The capital city of the United Arab Emirates; capital of Abu Dhabi emirate.
(historical) The Ethiopian Empire, a former empire in East Africa, consisting of modern-day Ethiopia and Eritrea.

(history) A colonial territory owned by France in the 17th and early 18th centuries, spanning over what are now the Maritime provinces of eastern Canada (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island) and part of the state of Maine in the USA.
The capital city of Ghana.

(Greek mythology) A mythical semidivine hero, the son of Peleus by the nereid Thetis, and prince of the Myrmidons, who features in the Iliad as a central character and the foremost warrior of the Achaean (Greek) camp.
A vulnerability in an otherwise strong situation.
(anatomy) The strong tendon formed of the united tendons of the large muscles in the calf of the leg, and inserted into the bone of the heel.
A port city in northern Israel, holiest city in the Baháʼí Faith.
A state of the North Region, Brazil. Capital: Rio Branco
(Abrahamism, religion) The first man and the progenitor of the human race.
A en given name.
The capital city of Ethiopia.
Pygoscelis adeliae, a species of penguin with distinctive white rings surrounding the eyes.
A river in South Tyrol, Italy.
(Greek mythology) A beautiful young man loved by Aphrodite.
A en given name.
(rare) A en given name (compare Adriana, Adrianna, Adrienne).
A sea and arm of the Mediterranean Sea, stretching north from the Ionian Sea to Venice, separating the Italian and Balkan Peninsulas.
A Northwest Caucasian language spoken in the Republic of Adygea, in the Russian Federation.
A sea in the northeastern part of the Mediterranean.
A classic epic poem, written in Latin by Virgil in the 1st century BCE (between 29 and 19 BCE), that tells the legendary story of Aeneas fleeing Troy and settling in Italy as ancestor of the Romans.
(Ancient Greece) A celebrated Greek statesman and orator (389–314 B.C.E.; full name Αἰσχίνης Ἀτρομήτου Κοθωκίδης, Aeschines Atrometi f. Cothocides), one the Canon of Ten Attic Orators.
A Greek dramatic poet (525 BCE—456 BCE); Aeschylus was the earliest of the three greatest Greek tragedians.
An Ancient Greek author, famous for the fables ascribed to him.
Of, from, or pertaining to Afghanistan.
A person from Afghanistan.
Synonym of Afghan Hound.
A landlocked country between Central Asia and South Asia. Official name: Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. Capital and largest city: Kabul.
The continent that is south of Europe, east of the Atlantic Ocean, west of the Indian Ocean and north of Antarctica.
A native of Africa; also one ethnologically belonging to an African race.
A multinational organisation consisting of 54 African nations.

A Germanic language descending from Dutch; the primary language of the descendants of Dutch and other European settlers, as well as many mixed-race (e.g. Rehoboth Basters) living in South Africa and in Namibia. Also, one of the eleven official languages of South Africa and until 1990 one of three official languages of Namibia.
A supercontinent that comprises Africa and Eurasia.
(historical period) A period of time ranging from part of the 17th century through much of the 18th century, characterized particularly by the importance of logic and reason.
A city in Greece located in the Aitolia-Akarnania prefecture.
One of the départements of Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, France. Capital: Bourg-en-Bresse (INSEE code 01)
Of or pertaining to the Ainu ethnic group or their language.
A member of an ethnic group on the northern Japanese island of Hokkaido.
The endangered language spoken by the Ainu ethnic group, generally considered a language isolate with no known relation to other languages.
(Greek god) A Hellenistic deity associated with time, the orb or circle encompassing the universe, and the zodiac.
One of the départements in Hauts-de-France, France. Capital: Laon (INSEE code 02)
A river in northern France, which flows into the Mayenne River
The capital and largest city of Corsica, France.
The Niger-Congo language spoken by these people.
A group of languages spoken in Ghana.
A state of the United States. Capital: Montgomery. Largest city: Birmingham.
The University of Alabama.
A state of the United States, formerly a territory. Capital: Juneau. Postal code: AK, largest city: Anchorage.
Several places in the United States, named for the state or territory.
A country in Southeast Europe. Official name: Republic of Albania. Capital and largest city: Tirana.
Of, from, or pertaining to Albania, the Albanian people or the Albanian language.
A person from Albania or of Albanian descent.
The languages spoken by the Albanian people, primarily spoken in Albania and Kosovo. (ISO 639 language codes: sq/sqi/alb (Albanian), als (Tosk), aln (Gheg), aat (Arvanitika), aae (Arbëresh).)
A en given name.
A province in western Canada. Capital: Edmonton.
A pine tree (Pinus halepensis), native to the Mediterranean basin.
A en given name, most famously held by Alexander the Great.
, a city in Piedmont, Italy.
A city in Clark County, Missouri.
A former town in the United Counties of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry, Ontario, Canada; now a part of the township of North Glengarry.
A city in Teleorman, Romania
A city in Greece and the capital of the Evros Prefecture in Thrace.
A country in North Africa. Official name: People's Democratic Republic of Algeria. Capital and largest city: Algiers.
The capital and largest city of Algeria.
A en given name popular in England since the Middle Ages.
God, in Islamic or Arabic contexts
One of the départements in Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, France. Capital: Moulins (INSEE code 03)
The countries allied against the Axis Powers during World War II. The major signatories included the United Kingdom, Soviet Union, United States, and China.
The countries allied against the Central Powers during World War I, including especially the United Kingdom, the Russian Empire, and France.
The largest city in and former (until 1998) capital of Kazakhstan, formerly known as Alma-Ata.
God, the supreme being.
One of the départements in Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France. Capital: Nice (INSEE code 05)

cit.quote: 上普罗旺斯阿尔卑斯省

sense.def: One of the départements in Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France. Capital: Digne-les-Bains (INSEE code 04).
(usually, with "the") A mountain range in Western Europe, running from France to Slovenia, the highest peak of which is Mont Blanc, at 4808 metres.

A region, former administrative region, and historical province of France, located on the west bank of the upper Rhine; since 2016, part of the administrative region of Grand Est. It has changed hands between France and Germany several times throughout history.
(with the) A mountain range in central Asia, where Russia, China, Mongolia and Kazakhstan converge.
A municipality, a town, the capital of Uri canton, Switzerland.
(Greek mythology) The most frequently mentioned foster mother of Zeus, sometimes represented as the goat who suckled the infant-god in a mountain cave, sometimes as a goat-tending nymph.
(sometimes, attributive) A region including much of this river; specifically, the region of the Amazon Rainforest, or of the Amazon River Basin.
A state of the North Region, Brazil. Capital: Manaus
The region of the Amazon rainforest.
(archaic) Synonym of American Indian or Native American, an indigenous inhabitant of the Americas. [from 16th c.]
A citizen or national of the United States of America.
A war fought in the United States between 1861 and 1865, between the Northern states (Union) and Southern states (Confederacy).
(idiomatic) A philosophy that with perseverance, courage and determination, anyone can prosper and achieve success.
The form of the English language that is chiefly used in the United States, contrasted with British English or Canadian English and that of other places.
An archipelago and overseas territory of the United States in the Pacific Ocean. Official name: Territory of American Samoa. It is distinct from Samoa (formerly: Western Samoa).
A sign language used primarily in the United States of America and Canada.
A bear of the species Ursus americanus, native to cooler climates in North America.

A game similar to rugby football played on a field of 100 yards long and 53 1/3 yards wide (with two 10 yard-long endzones) in which two teams of 11 players attempt to get an ovoid ball into each other's territory.
(US, Canada) To render American; to adapt to the custom, culture, or style of the United States of America.
North America and South America taken together; that is, North America, Central America, and South America taken together.
A Semitic language spoken in Ethiopia.
In Vajrayāna Buddhism, the name of the western buddha, one of the Five Dhyani Buddhas representing the five qualities of the Buddha.
The capital city of Jordan.
A governorate of Jordan around the capital.
A book of the Old Testament and the Hebrew Tanakh.
A city and municipality of North Holland, Netherlands; capital city of the Netherlands.

The world's ninth-longest river, forming part of the border between the Far East of Russia and Northeastern China, emptying into the Pacific Ocean through the Strait of Tartary, where the mouth of the river faces the northern end of the island of Sakhalin.
The doctrine espoused by Anabaptists.
A en given name.

A peninsula in Western Asia, comprising most of the modern Republic of Turkey. Bounded by the Black Sea to the north, the Armenian Highland to the east, the Mediterranean Sea to the south and the Aegean Sea to the west.

The civilization that flourished around the Mediterranean Sea from the 3rd millennium to the 1st century BCE (including the first two European civilizations, Minoan and Mycenaean), known as the cradle of Western civilization.
Any of the various forms of the Greek language of classical antiquity, particularly the classical Attic dialect used in Athenian literature.
The most populated and second largest of the seventeen autonomous communities that constitute Spain, whose capital is Seville.
Part of the Indian Ocean, to the southeast of the Bay of Bengal, south of Burma (Myanmar), west of Thailand, north-west of the Malay Peninsula, north of Sumatra, and east of the Andaman Islands.
A South American bird in the New World vulture family Cathartidae, Vultur gryphus.
A mountain range in western South America.
A state in southeastern India, where Telugu is the primary language. Capital: Amaravati.
A microstate in Southern Europe, between Spain and France. Official name: Principality of Andorra. Capital and largest city: Andorra la Vella.
The capital city of Andorra
(countable) A en given name.
The first Apostle in the New Testament.
(Greek mythology) the wife of Hector

(Greek mythology) The daughter of Cepheus and Cassiopeia, king and queen of Eritrea, rescued from her sacrifice to the sea monster Cetus by Perseus, who married her; mother of Perses, ancient king of Persia.

(constellation) A constellation of the northern sky representing the "chained woman" Andromeda in Greek mythology, which is surrounded by the constellations of Cassiopeia, Perseus, and Pegasus, among others.
A river in Russia.
A en given name.
A en given name.
A region of Schleswig-Holstein, Germany.
The beliefs and practices of the Anglican Church.
A combining form relating to the English or British people, culture, or livestock.
Related to the Anglo-Saxon peoples or language.
The totality of Anglophone countries, the geographical or cultural realm of native English-speakers.
Synonym of angora (cat).
An archipelago and overseas territory of the United Kingdom, in the Caribbean Sea.
The capital city of Turkey.
A en given name.
(history) One the French protectorates in Vietnam, located in Central Vietnam.
In the year of our Lord (often abbreviated A.D. or AD).
The capital city of Madagascar.
Of, from, or pertaining to Antarctica and the south polar regions.

One of the major ecozones of the world, covering the south polar regions. Especially those south of the Antarctic Convergence or the 60th parallel south (everywhere south of this parallel being administered by the Antarctic Treaty System).
The southernmost continent, south of the Southern Ocean, containing the South Pole.
(star) Alpha Scorpii (α Sco), the brightest star in the constellation Scorpius. It is a M type red giant, and is a binary with a B type companion visible in greenish.
(historical) A medieval European tribal union who lived north of the lower Danube and the Black Sea (on the territory of modern Moldova and Ukraine) in the 6th and 7th century AD.
A en given name, in regular use since the Middle Ages.

(geology, formal, strictly) A proposed but rejected geological epoch, in which the effect of human activities on the global environment has disrupted the natural variability of the Holocene, ending the Holocene. (It was rejected as formal scientific nomenclature in 2024 owing to not meeting a bar for how a geological epoch is formally defined.) [from 1960s]
(Christianity, Islam) A false messiah who, under direct control of the Devil, will usher in the abomination in the end times; a false prophet.
A country in the Caribbean, consisting of the islands of Antigua and Barbuda.
A Greek island located between Peloponnese and Crete, near Kythira.
The period of Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome.
(constellation) A faint winter constellation of the northern sky, said to resemble a pump. The common English name is "Air pump".
a Roman nomen gentile
A province of Flanders, Belgium, the most populous.
The second-largest city in Belgium, and the capital of its province.
(Egyptian god) In the mythology of ancient Egypt, the god of the dead and tombs, commonly depicted with the head of a jackal.
A river in Zhejiang, China
A river in Fujian, China
A mountain range in Italy, stretching 1,200 km from the north to the south of the country, along its east coast, traversing the entire Apennine Peninsula, and often called the "spine of Italy".
(Greek god) The goddess of beauty and love, born when Cronus castrated his father, Uranus, and threw his genitalia into the sea. Her Roman counterpart is Venus.
(countable, biblical) The written account of a revelation of hidden things given by God to a chosen prophet.
(Christianity) Revelation (last book of the Bible, composed of twenty-two chapters, which narrates the end of times)

(astronomy) An asteroid possessing an orbit that crosses the orbit of the Earth and an orbital period of over one year, with semimajor axes greater than 1 AU, and perihelion distances less than 1.017 AU.

(Greek god, Roman god) The son of Zeus and Leto (or Jupiter and Latona), and the twin brother of Artemis (or Diana). He was the god of light, music, medicine, and poetry; and prophecy, dance, manly beauty, and more.
(Christianity) Any of the group of twelve disciples chosen by Jesus to preach and spread the Gospel.

A range of mountains in eastern North America, running northeast from Alabama in the United States to Newfoundland in Canada, variously including or excluding the Adirondack Mountains in northern New York.
The fourth month of the Gregorian calendar, following March and preceding May. Abbreviation: Apr or Apr.
The first day in April, when tricks and practical jokes are traditionally played
A practical joke played on April Fools' Day.
A peninsula and administrative region in southern Italy.
(constellation) A constellation of the southern sky, said to resemble a bird of paradise.
A city in Jordan, on the Red Sea.
(zodiac constellations) A constellation of the zodiac, supposedly shaped like a water carrier.
(astrology) The zodiac sign for the water carrier, ruled by Uranus covering January 20 – February 18 (tropical astrology) or February 15 – March 14 (sidereal astrology).
(constellation) A summer constellation of the northern sky, said to resemble an eagle. It includes the star Altair.
(historical) A former administrative region of France, now part of Nouvelle-Aquitaine.
(constellation) A constellation of the southern sky, said to resemble an altar.
A Semitic person, whose forebears were from the Arabian Peninsula
The official name of the country of Egypt.
A peninsula of Western Asia between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf; includes Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and the United Arab Emirates.
Related to Arabia.
A native of Arabia.
An Arabian horse.

A peninsula in the Middle East, bordered by Jordan, the Syrian desert and Iraq to the north, the Persian Gulf to the northeast, the Gulf of Oman to the east, the Arabian Sea (part of the Indian Ocean) to the south (southeast), the Gulf of Aden to the south, the Red Sea to the west (southwest) extending north into the Gulf of Aqaba, and north along the Red Sea Rift to the Mediterranean Sea on the west (northwest). It consists mainly of Saudi Arabia, and may be geologically defined as the Arabian plate, also as the Arabian subcontinent.
Of, from, or pertaining to Arab countries or cultural behaviour (see also Arab as an adjective).
The Aramaic-derived alphabet used to write the Arabic, Persian, Pashto, Urdu, and Uyghur languages, among others.
(in the plural) The system using such numerals, now employed throughout the world.
(transitive) To make Arab; to give Arab traits to.
Of, from, or pertaining to Aragon, the Aragonese people or the Aragonese language.
A person from Aragon.
The language of Aragon, nowadays only spoken as a mother tongue by a few thousand people in some valleys of the Pyrenees.

A saline lake, straddling the Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan border, that was once large, but shrank to a quarter of its original size after the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, which previously flowed into it, were diverted for irrigation purposes during the Soviet era.

Any member of a West Semitic semi-nomadic and pastoralist people who lived in the Levant and later also in upper Mesopotamia (Biblical Aram) during the Late Bronze Age and the Iron Age. They spoke Aramaic.
Referring to the Aramaic language, alphabet, culture or poetry.
The language of the Aramaeans from the tenth century BC: often called Old Aramaic.
Pertaining to the Arawak peoples
(figurative) An ideal region of rural and idyllic contentment; a pastoral utopia.
An Ancient Greek mathematician, physicist and engineer (c. 287–212 BCE).
(geography) Pertaining to the northern polar region of the planet, characterised by extreme cold and an icy landscape. [from 16th c.]
Extremely cold, snowy, or having other properties of extreme winter associated with the Arctic. [from 16th c.]
(geography) The region of the Earth above the Arctic Circle, containing the North Pole. [from 17th c.]
The smallest of the five oceans of the Earth, on and around the North Pole, bordered by the three continents of Asia, Europe and North America.
(star) A bright yellow-orange star in the constellation Boötes; Alpha (α) Boötis. It is the fourth-brightest star in the night sky.
A department of Grand Est, France. Capital: Charleville-Mézières (INSEE code 08)
forest and mountainous region in France, Belgium, Germany and Luxembourg.
A department in Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, south-central France. Capital: Privas.
A river in south-central France that gives its name to the department.
(Greek god) The Greek god of war, considered equivalent to the Roman Mars and usually described as a son of Zeus and Hera, companion of Eris and Enyo, and by Aphrodite father of Deimos and Phobos.
A country in South America. Official name: Argentine Republic. Capital: Buenos Aires.
A citizen or descendant abroad of Argentina.
(dance) Short for Argentine tango.
The official name of Argentina.
(astronomy) The brightest moon of the planet Uranus.
Someone with an Aries star sign.
(zodiac constellations) A constellation of the zodiac supposedly shaped like a ram.
(astrology) The zodiac sign for the ram, ruled by Mars and covering March 20 – April 20 (tropical astrology) or April 15 – May 15 (sidereal astrology).
An Ancient Greek male name, most famously borne by a playwright who lived from circa 446 BC to circa 386 BC.
(philosophy) The philosophical system of Aristotle (384 BCE – 322 BCE) and his followers.
An ancient Greek philosopher, logician, and scientist (382–322 BCE), student of Plato and teacher of Alexander the Great.
(historical) A territory of the southwest Confederate (1862–1865) and United States of America (1863–1912), with its capitals at Tucson, Prescott, and Phoenix.
One of the départements in Occitanie, France (INSEE code 09)
A state in the South Central region of the United States. Capital and largest city: Little Rock.
A city in the Bouches-du-Rhône department, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France.
(historical) Ancient kingdom in the Armenian Highland southeast of Black Sea and southwest of Caspian Sea; area now divided between Turkey, Republic of Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Iran.
Of, from, or pertaining to Armenia, the Armenian people, the Armenian language, or the Armenian alphabet.
(countable) A person from Armenia or of Armenian descent.
(uncountable) A branch of Indo-European languages, which includes the various stages of the Armenian language.
A en given name occasionally used in English.
A river in Tuscany that flows through Pisa and Florence.
A decorative style of art and architecture that especially used the sinuous and flowing lines of plants.
(Greek god) The Greek goddess of the hunt, wild animals, and wilderness; the daughter of Leto and Zeus; the sister of Apollo. (Compare Diana.)
A en given name.
An island, dependent territory, and constituent country of the Netherlands, in the Caribbean Sea.
(Christianity, specifically) The believed entry of Jesus Christ into heaven after his resurrection.
The fortieth day of Easter, that is the Thursday 39 days after Easter.

(Greek god) A Greek mythological deity, the god of doctors, medicine and healing; a son of Apollo and the Thessalian princess Coronis, husband to the goddess Epione and father of the Asclepiades; identified with the Roman god Aesculapius.
(Christianity) The Wednesday 46 days before Easter in a given year, (Catholicism) traditionally observed as the beginning of Lent and a day of strict abstention from certain foods and pleasures.
The capital and largest city of Turkmenistan.
(history) The Turkic tribe who served as the ruling dynasty of the Göktürks during the First and Second Turkic Khaganates (552–603 and 682–744, respectively).
A continent located east of Europe (typically delimited by the Urals), west of the Pacific Ocean, north of Oceania and south of the Arctic Ocean.
An ancient province of the Roman Empire, in modern western Turkey.
Of, relating to or from Asia.
(UK, Ireland, South Africa) A person from or with ancestry in South Asia.
(US, Canada, Australia, NZ, also International English on the Internet) A person from or with ancestry in East or Southeast Asia, occasionally South Asia.
A person from the continent of Asia, or a descendant thereof - especially:
A large conical hat popular in some Asian countries, made of bamboo or straw.
The capital city of Eritrea.

(dated, uncountable, neurology) An autism-related developmental disorder characterised by sustained impairment in social interaction and nonverbal communication and by repetitive behaviour as well as restricted interests and routines.
A state in northeastern India. Capital: Dispur.
The Indo-Aryan language spoken by the majority people in the state of Assam, NE India.

A Semitic Akkadian kingdom, extant from the mid-23rd century BC to 608 BC and centred on the Upper Tigris river in northern Mesopotamia (present day northern Iraq), which came to rule regional empires a number of times through history.
The capital city of Kazakhstan.
A series of French comic books written by René Goscinny and illustrated by Albert Uderzo about an Ancient Gaul named Asterix.
A city, the administrative center of Astrakhan Oblast, Russia, located on the Volga River.
(history) A former kingdom in northwestern Spain
(archaic) Asturias
A Romance language spoken in Asturias, Spain.
An autonomous community and province of Spain, on the Spanish north coast facing the Cantabrian Sea. The capital city is Oviedo.
The capital city of Paraguay.
The capital of Aswan governorate, Egypt
An Austronesian people of Taiwan.
(Greek god) The goddess of wisdom, especially strategic warfare, the arts, and especially crafts, in particular, weaving; daughter of Zeus and Metis. Her Roman counterpart is Minerva.
The capital city of Greece.
The capital city, the county seat of Fulton County, Georgia, United States.
The ocean lying between the Americas to the west and Europe and Africa to the east.
A mythical country said to have sunk into the Atlantic Ocean.

(Greek god) The son of Iapetus and Clymene, war leader of the Titans ordered by the god Zeus to support the sky on his shoulders; father to the Hesperides, the Hyades, and the Pleiades; king of the legendary Atlantis.
(astronomy) A crater in the last quadrant of the moon.
(astronomy) A moon of Saturn.
(rocketry, military, US) An SM-65, an early ICBM, soon developed into a long-lived orbital launch vehicle series.
A periphery where Athens, the capital of Greece, is located.
(historical) Attila, kingly ruler of the tribe of the Huns and vast Eurasian Hunnic Empire and feared enemy of the Roman Empire, from 434 until his death in 453.
A department of Grand Est, France (INSEE code 10).
A tributary of the Seine, France.
A city in New Zealand's North Island, the largest conurbation in the country.
A region of New Zealand which includes the city, situated between the Northland region to the north and the Waikato region to the south.
A department of Occitanie, France. Capital: Carcassonne.
A river in the Aude department, France.
An independent city, the administrative seat of Swabia, Bavaria, in southern Germany
The eighth month of the Roman, Julian, and Gregorian calendars, following July and preceding September.
The Roman emperor Augustus, also called Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus (63 B.C.E. – 14 C.E.); heir to Julius Caesar
A en given name, risen in popularity since the 18th century.

A surname originating as an occupation derived from the trade name carpenter.

(set theory, of two sets X and Y) The set of all possible ordered pairs of elements, the being first from X, the second from Y, written X \times Y. Formally, the set \{(x,y)\; |\; x\in X \; \text{and} \; y\in Y\}.
(historical) An ancient city in North Africa, in modern Tunisia. [16th cent.]
A native or inhabitant of Carthage.
The capital city of the region of Casablanca-Settat, Morocco
A landlocked sea (properly a saline lake) between Eastern Europe and Asia, and the Earth’s largest inland body of water.
(Greek mythology) Proud wife of Cepheus and mother of Andromeda, queen of Ethiopia. When she boasted that her beauty was equal to that of the Nereids, she was punished by Poseidon.

(constellation) A circumpolar constellation of the northern sky representing Queen Cassiopeia from Greek myth. The constellation lies between Cepheus and Perseus and contains the stars Schedar and Caph.
A medieval kingdom (and previously a county) in the Iberian Peninsula.
A vaguely defined region of central Spain generally corresponding to the regions of Old and New Castile.
The largest of the autonomous communities of Spain, in the central north of the country.
(Greek mythology) One of the Dioscuri
(star) A double star in the constellation Gemini; alpha (α) Geminorum.
The capital city of Saint Lucia.
Of or pertaining to Catalonia.
A native or inhabitant of Catalonia.

The Romance language of Catalonia, an autonomous region in the northeast of Spain, also spoken in the Valencian autonomous region (where the language is officially named valencià), the Balearic Islands, Andorra, Roussillon in France, and the Sardinian city of Alghero.

The territories where Catalan is spoken, and these regions are Catalonia, Valencian Community, the Balearic Islands, the Aragon Strip and the Carxe (in Spain), the Northern Catalonia (in France), the Alghero (in Italy), and Andorra.
A name given to the country that will be formed in a hypothetical and independent political union of all Catalan-speaking regions.
An autonomous community of Spain.
(idiomatic) A difficult situation from which there is no escape because it involves mutually conflicting or dependent conditions.
A en given name.
The faiths, practices and doctrines of the Catholic Church, usually the Roman Catholic Church.
A native or inhabitant of the Caucasus.
(anthropology, dated) A member of the Caucasian racial classification (adjective sense 2).
(geopolitical) A geopolitical region in Eastern Europe and Western Asia, deriving its name from the aforementioned mountains.
The capital city of the French Guiana department.
Three islands in the Caribbean Sea constituting an overseas territory of the United Kingdom.
Pertaining to the Cebuano language or to its speakers.
A language spoken in the Philippines in and near the province of Cebu.
(historical) A member of one of the ancient peoples of Western Europe called Celtae by the Romans.

(geology) A geologic era within the Phanerozoic eon comprising the Paleogene, Neogene and Quaternary periods from about 65 million years ago to the present, when the continents moved to their current position and modern plants and animals evolved.

(constellation) A spring constellation of the northern sky (and autumn of the southern sky) with the outline of a centaur. It includes the stars Alpha Centauri (Rigil Kentaurus and Toliman), Proxima Centauri, and Hadar.
(historical) The Central African Republic state from 1976 to 1979.
A country in Central Africa.
The part of continental North America which lies between Mexico and South America.
A landlocked area of continental Asia comprising Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. In the USSR and the modern Russia, the area is called Middle Asia (Средняя Азия).
A geographic region in the center of Europe, usually including Austria, Switzerland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia and Germany.
An island of Greece in the eastern Ionian Sea, the largest of the Ionian Islands.
(Greek mythology) Husband of Cassiopeia, king of Eritrea, father of Andromeda. There may be two mythical kings by this name.
(Greek mythology) The giant three-headed dog who guards the entrance to Hades; and one of the many offspring of Echidna and Typhon.
(Roman god) The Roman goddess of agriculture; equivalent to the Greek goddess Demeter.
(astronomy) A celestial body orbiting between Mars and Jupiter, the innermost dwarf planet; officially called (1) Ceres. (see usage notes)
(constellation) A winter constellation of the northern sky, said to resemble a whale. It includes the star Mira.
A country in Central Africa. Official name: Republic of Chad.
Lake Chad (a freshwater lake at the junction of Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon in Central Africa).
An ancient maritime town of Bithynia, in Asia Minor in modern Turkey, almost directly opposite Byzantium.
(constellation) A small circumpolar constellation of the southern sky, imagined to resemble a chameleon, which lies south of the constellations Carina and Musca.
region of France
(soccer) The highest-level European club football (soccer) tournament, organised by UEFA.
One of the kings of the Franks from 768 to 814, crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 800 until his death in 814.
The largest city of Wallonia, in the province of Hainaut, Belgium.
A en given name.
A en given name.
(astronomy) The largest of the five moons of Pluto.
The capital and largest city of Chuvashia, Russia.
The language of the Chechens, a member of the Nakh family.
A republic of the northern Caucasus of Russia. Official name: Chechen Republic. Capital: Grozny.
A city, the administrative center of Chelyabinsk Oblast, Russia.
An independent city in Saxony, Germany.
A subprovincial city, the provincial capital of Sichuan, in southwestern China.
A partially abandoned city and ghost town in northern Ukraine, known as the site of a nuclear disaster.
A large city, the county seat of Cook County, in northeastern Illinois, United States, located on Lake Michigan.
The smallest breed of dog in the world, originating in Mexico and having large erect ears.
A country in South America. Official name: Republic of Chile. Capital and largest city: Santiago.
(Greek mythology) A supposed fire-breathing monster in Lycia with the head of a lion, body of a goat, and tail of a dragon or snake, killed by the hero Bellerophon.
A nation or civilization occupying the country around the Yellow, Yangtze, and Pearl Rivers in East Asia, taken as a whole under its various dynasties.
The principal state in this country, including (historical) an empire under various dynasties and (since 1949) the People's Republic of China.
China excluding Inner Mongolia, Manchuria, Mongolia, Taiwan, Tibet, Tuva, and Xinjiang.
(dated, now, offensive) A Chinese person, or person of Chinese descent.
Of, from, or related to a language native to Han Chinese persons, often used generally of Chinese characters or particularly to refer to Standard Mandarin.
(countable, chiefly, in the plural) A person/people from China or of Chinese descent.
(uncountable, collective) The citizens of China, particularly citizens of the People's Republic of China.
(uncountable) The branch of the Sino-Tibetan language family including Mandarin, Cantonese, Shanghainese, Southern Min, and other closely related language varieties and dialects.
An annual Chinese holiday, marking the beginning of a new year according to the traditional Chinese calendar.
A name under which the Republic of China (Taiwan) participates in international organisations.
Any character used in the written form of several languages of China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam.
A board game played by two to six people, in which players aim to move their own pieces to the corner opposite their starting position by single moves or jumps over other pieces.
A gall produced by the Chinese sumac (Rhus chinensis) when infested by the female Chinese sumac aphid (Schlechtendalia chinensis).
A rare species of ragwort, Sinacalia tangutica, endemic to China
(humanities) An academic discipline that includes the study of literature written in the Chinese language, Chinese linguistics, and Chinese sociolinguistics.

(games, mostly, UK) A game for several players in which a phrase, whispered by each person in turn to their neighbour, is often unwittingly misunderstood as it is transferred, to humorous effect by the time it reaches the last person and is compared with the original phrase.
(Greek mythology) An old, wise centaur who served as Achilles' mentor and teacher.
(astronomy, astrology) A centaur (minor planet) and comet-like/asteroid-like object, orbiting between Saturn and Uranus.
A municipality, the capital city of Moldova.
A direct-administered municipality and city in western China.
(Christianity) The anointed one, the Messiah predicted by the Old Testament.
(Christianity) A title given to Jesus of Nazareth, seen as the fulfiller of the messianic prophecy.
A member of a particular nontrinitarian Christian denomination founded in the mid-19th century.
(not comparable) Of, like or relating to Christianity or Christians.
(obsolete, England) A European, especially though not necessarily of the Christian religion.
(Christianity) A first name formally given to a child at a Christian baptism.
An Abrahamic religion originating from the community of the followers of Jesus Christ.
A diminutive of the en given name Christine and of its variant forms; fairly common as a formal female given name in the 20th century.
A surname originating as a patronymic derived from Christopher or Christian.

(originally, Christianity) A festival or holiday commemorating the birth of Jesus Christ and incorporating various Christian, pre-Christian, pagan, and secular customs, which in Western Christianity is celebrated on December 25 (Christmas Day) in most places.
The day on which Christmas is celebrated. It is December 25 in the West, and January 7 in some Eastern Orthodox churches.
A non-self-governing territory of Australia, located in the Indian Ocean.
(music genre) A carol (song or hymn) whose lyrics are on the theme of Christmas.
A conifer used during the Christmas holiday season, typically decorated with lights and ornaments and often a star or angel at its tip.
A en given name.
A surname originating as a patronymic.

An agglutinative language of the Bolgar branch of the Turkic language family and is spoken west of the Ural mountains in central Russia. Chuvash is the native language of the Chuvash people and an official language of Chuvashia. It is spoken by about two million people.
The Roman statesman and orator Mārcus Tullius Cicerō (106–43 BC).
A popular fairy tale embodying a classic folk tale myth-element of unjust oppression and triumphant reward.
The main character in this story, a mistreated and impoverished girl.
(constellation) A small constellation of the southern winter sky, said to resemble a compass. It lies between the constellations of Centaurus and Triangulum Australe.

The written Chinese language used from the Zhou Dynasty (1045 B.C.E.) (especially the Spring and Autumn Period), through to the end of the Han Dynasty (220 C.E.). In Chinese, or, formally, . The language of many classics of Chinese literature.
The written Chinese language used from the Zhou Dynasty (1045 B.C.E.) to the early 20th century.
The variants of the Nahuatl language spoken in central Mexico at the time of the Spanish colonization.
A given name of women in the Ptolemaic dynasty of Egypt; notably Queen Cleopatra VII of Egypt (69–30 BCE); last of the Ptolemy line.
(Greek god) The goddess of history and heroic poetry, and one of the Muses; the daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne.
A particular cola soft drink (type of carbonated drink), produced by the Coca-Cola Company.
A surname from Irish [in turn originating as a patronymic].
(computing) A Business Intelligence technology, produced by Canadian company Cognos software, which was bought by IBM.
(countable, uncountable, informal) Cola-based soft drink; (in particular) Coca-Cola.
(US, especially, Southern US, informal) Any soft drink, regardless of type.
(historical) The period of hostility short of open war between the Soviet Bloc and the Western powers, especially the United States, between 1945 and 1991.
The largest city in North Rhine-Westphalia, in northwestern Germany, on the Rhine River.
A country in South America. Official name: Republic of Colombia. Capital: Bogotá.
The commercial capital and largest city of Sri Lanka.
A state in the western United States, the 38th state. Capital and largest city: Denver.
(constellation) A small winter constellation of the northern sky, said to resemble a dove.
District of Columbia The federal capital region of the United States of America, including Washington, D.C.

(constellation) A small dim summer constellation of the northern sky, said to represent an offering of hair from Queen Berenice II of Egypt. Originally considered to represent the tuft of hair on the end of Leo's tail.

An association of independent, sovereign states most of which formerly constituted the British Empire.
The official name of the state of Bahamas.
A country and group of islands in the Indian Ocean off the coast of East Africa. Official name: Union of the Comoros.

Congo, Democratic Republic of the Congo (a country in Central Africa, larger and to the east of the Republic of the Congo; official name: Democratic Republic of the Congo; capital: Kinshasa).
Congo, Republic of the Congo (a country in Central Africa, smaller and to the west of the Democratic Republic of the Congo; official name: Republic of the Congo; capital: Brazzaville).
A large river in Africa which flows for about 4,380 km (2,720 miles) to the Atlantic Ocean in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The two legislative bodies of the United States: the House of Representatives and the Senate.
A en given name.
Name of present-day Istanbul from 330–1930 C.E.. Previously known as Byzantium.
An archipelago and self-governing country in Oceania, in free association with New Zealand.
The capital city of Denmark.
A member of the Coptic Church.
Of or pertaining to the Copts, the Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria or to the Coptic language.
The Afroasiatic language traditionally spoken by the Copts in Egypt, now extinct and used only as a liturgical language.
A marginal sea of the Pacific Ocean off the north-east coast of Australia.
An island in Greece, one of the Ionian Islands. The ancient name is Corcyra (Κόρκυρα), in Modern Greek Kérkira (Κέρκυρα).
The capital of Corfu.
Of or pertaining to Cornwall, a county of southwest England.
The Celtic language of Cornwall, related to Welsh and Breton.

The country of the Cornish, currently having the status of a royal duchy in England belonging to the male heir apparent to the reigning monarch, and consisting at least of the Cornwall County and the Isles of Scilly.
The westernmost of the three historical counties of Jamaica, bordered by the county of Middlesex in the east; named for the English county.
(constellation) A small summer constellation of the northern sky said to resemble a crown.

the language of the Corsican people

A country in Central America. Official name: Republic of Costa Rica.

Province of Lombardy, Italy.

Synonym of Crimean peninsula: A peninsula in the Black Sea, Europe, officially part of Ukraine, annexed by Russia. A peninsula which juts southwards out of the Ukrainian mainland (to which it is connected by the Isthmus of Perekop) into the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, separating the Sea of Azov from the Black Sea.

(historical) Synonym of Crimean Khanate: A historical country in Crimean Peninsula, Europe. The Crimean Khanate, which for much of its history controlled most of the Crimean peninsula and various adjacent areas of the mainland.

Any of a series of religious campaigns by Christian forces from the 11th to the 13th century, mostly to capture the Holy Land from the Muslims who occupied it.

A gigantic fictional humanoid alien god being described with a head resembling an octopus and dragon wings and claws, around whom an insane cult developed.
A country, and the largest island (based on land area) in the Caribbean. Capital and largest city: Havana.

(informal, sports) A win of a championship that is awarded a cup.

An island and country in the Mediterranean Sea, normally considered politically part of Southeast Europe but geographically part of Western Asia. Official name: Republic of Cyprus. Capital: Nicosia.

Denoting an alphabet devised for writing the Old Church Slavonic liturgical language, and its adaptations used for several languages of Eastern Europe and Asia; of or relating to this writing system.

A republic of Russia, located in the Caucasus region. Capital: Makhachkala
The capital city of Senegal.

Gdańsk (especially in reference to the times when it was part of a German-speaking state such as Prussia or Germany).

The variety of the Persian language that is chiefly used in Afghanistan, contrasted with varieties spoken elsewhere such as Iranian Persian or Tajik.

A river in Eastern Europe, flowing through Russia, Belarus and Latvia to the Gulf of Riga.
A borough in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania, United States.
A city in Manitoba, Canada.
A commune of the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence department, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France.
(biblical character) The second king of Judah and Israel, the successor of King Saul in the Old Testament; the son of Jesse and the father of Nathan and King Solomon.
(rare) A en given name, often combined with a feminine middle name (e.g. David Ann).

The Dayi method, a text-input method for Chinese characters invented after the Cāngjié method and designed to be faster. Like Cāngjié, this system is based on the character shape rather than phonetics.
A lake in the Middle East in Israel, Palestine and Jordan, noted for high salinity and for its banks being the lowest land-based elevation on Earth.
The personification of death, often a skeleton with a scythe, and one of the four horsemen of the apocalypse.
The twelfth and last month of the Gregorian calendar, following November and preceding the January of the following year, containing the southern solstice.
(Greek mythology) A son of Ares (Latin: Mars), god of terror.
(astronomy) The outermost natural satellite of Mars.

A religious philosophy and movement prominent in 17th-18th-century England, France, and what is now the United States which rejected supernatural events such as prophecy and miracles, divine revelation, and holy books or revealed religions that assert such things exist.
A member of the Lenape / Delaware people.
The Lenape people, the indigenous people of Lenapehoking, in what is now the Mid-Atlantic United States.

A country in Central Africa. Capital: Kinshasa.
A Greek philosopher (c.460-c.370 BC). The originator of the atomic theory together with his teacher Leucippus.

A country in Europe. Official name: Kingdom of Denmark. Capital and largest city: Copenhagen.
A town and local government area (Shire of Denmark) in the Great Southern region, Western Australia.

Othello's wife in Shakespeare's play The Tragedy of Othello, the Moor of Venice, noted for being a victim of jealousy.
(astronomy) An inner moon of the planet Uranus.

The fifth of the Books of Moses in the Old Testament of the Bible, the fifth book in the Torah.

An abugida script used to write many languages originating in India and Nepal, including Sanskrit, Hindi, Marathi, Kashmiri, Sindhi, Maithili, Bhili, Konkani, Bhojpuri, and Nepali.
An Indo-Aryan language, the official language of the Republic of Maldives.

A famous 1605–1615 Spanish novel by Miguel de Cervantes (1547–1616), whose full title is El ingenioso hidalgo don Quijote de la Mancha (The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha).
One of the Disney cartoon characters, an anthropomorphic white-feathered duck who usually wears a sailor suit and is known for his voice especially in tantrums.
(usually with definite article) An industrial region in eastern Ukraine.
(city and raion) A city, administrative centre, and raion of Donetsk Oblast, in the Donbas region, in eastern Ukraine, on the Kalmius river.

A river running through Switzerland and France, a tributary of the Saône.
A department in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, France. Capital: Besançon.

A fictional city, located in the fictional US state of Calisota, that serves as the home of Donald Duck, his surrounding cast, and several other anthropomorphic animals.

The capital city of Tajikistan.

The third planet of the Solar System; the world upon which humans live.
The Eastern world; the regions, primarily situated in the Eastern Hemisphere, whose culture is derived from Arabia, India, Persia or China.
The Eastern Bloc; the eastern countries of Europe.
The eastern part of Asia inclusive of China proper, Japan, North Korea, South Korea, and Taiwan and sometimes inclusive of Mongolia and Tibet and some or all of Southeast Asia and the Philippines.

A country in Southeast Asia occupying half the island of Timor. Official name: Democratic Republic of Timor-Leste. Capital: Dili.

A Christian feast commemorating the resurrection of Jesus Christ, celebrated on the first Sunday (and Monday) following the full moon that occurs on or next after the vernal equinox, ranging in most of Western Christianity (such as Protestantism and Roman Catholicism) from March 22 to April 25, and in Eastern Christianity (such as the Coptic Church and Eastern Orthodox Church) from April 4 to May 8.
A symbolic rabbit sometimes depicted delivering Easter eggs to children.
An island in the South Pacific, belonging to Chile and famous for its moai monuments.
A dyed or decorated egg, traditionally associated with Easter and, in the Western European tradition, sometimes hidden for children to find.

Pertaining to the country of Malaysia.
Pertaining to the Malay language.
A native of Malaysia.
An archipelago and country in South Asia, located in the Indian Ocean off the coast of India. Official name: Republic of Maldives. Capital: Malé.
A country in West Africa. Official name: Republic of Mali.
A city in Scania, Sweden; the third-largest city in the country, located on the south-west coast.
An island country in Southern Europe. Capital: Valletta.
The archipelago in the Mediterranean Sea composing the country.
The largest island in the Maltese Archipelago.
A small city, the county seat of Phillips County, Montana, United States.

The Semitic language of Malta.
The capital city of the Maldives.
The genus Homo.
A city, the capital city of Bahrain.
A municipality, the state capital of Amazonas, Brazil.
A department of Normandy, France. Capital: Saint-Lô.

A person belonging to or descended from the indigenous people of Manchuria.

The capital city of the Philippines; regional capital of Metro Manila, in the island of Luzon.
The fibre of the abaca.
A province in Western Canada.
Province of Lombardy, Italy.
City and capital of Mantua.
(uncountable) A Goidelic language spoken on the Isle of Man.
Of, from, or pertaining to the Maori.

A person of a Marathi-speaking people from the state of Maharashtra; a person of or from Maharashtra.
An Indo-Aryan language that is the predominant language spoken in the state of Maharashtra, India.
A town in Attica, Greece, the site of the victory in 490 BC of heavily outnumbered Athenians against Persians.
The third month of the Gregorian calendar, following February and preceding April. Abbreviation: Mar or Mar.
An administrative region in central Italy.
A en given name.
A en given name.

The capital city of the Marrakesh-Safi region, Morocco.

The socialist and communist philosophy and political program founded by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels.

The socialist and communist theory of the followers of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels; a radical, revolutionary political philosophy that aims to capture state power, introduce a dictatorship of the proletariat, and then progress to communism.

(Roman Catholic Church) The principal liturgical service of the Church, encompassing both a scripture service (Liturgy of the Word) and a eucharistic service (Liturgy of the Eucharist), which includes the consecration and oblation (offering) of the host and wine.
An area in northeastern Poland, historically part of East Prussia.
A en given name.
A en given name of biblical origin.

A city and municipality in Antwerp province, Belgium.

The capital city of Victoria, Australia and former capital of Australia (1901–1927).
(biblical character) A king and priest mentioned in the book of Genesis; contemporary of Abraham.
A en given name. Popular in the latter half of the 20th century.
(UK, Canada, Australia, NZ) A representative elected by the voters of an electoral district to a house of a parliament.
A river in Lithuania that runs by this city; the Neman.
A Chinese surname from Mandarin.

Of, from, or pertaining to the country of Mexico.
A person from the country of Mexico or of Mexican descent.

The most famous Disney cartoon character, an anthropomorphic mouse with a falsetto voice and a cheerful disposition.
(constellation) A faint constellation of the southern spring sky, said to resemble a microscope. It lies south of the constellation of Capricornus.

(galaxy) The Milky Way Galaxy, the galaxy in which Earth is located. [from mid 19th c.]
(countable) An English and Scottish surname originating as an occupation for a miller.
(Greek mythology) A son of Gaia; one of the Gigantes.
An Ancient Egyptian god of fertility and procreation.

A Kartvelian language spoken in parts of Georgia (mainly Samegrelo and Abkhazia).
The capital city of Belarus.
One of the moons of Uranus.
Form of address, now used chiefly for an unmarried woman; used chiefly of girls before the mid-1700s, and thereafter used also of adult women without regard to marital status.

Moldavia, Western Moldavia (a region in eastern Romania adjacent to the country of Moldova, once part of the principality of Moldova).

Relating to the country of Moldova.
Relating to the Moldovan language.
An inhabitant of the Republic of Moldova.
The dialect of Romanian spoken in the Republic of Moldova, which may be written in either the Cyrillic or the Roman alphabet.

A crude incendiary bomb made from a glass bottle, either filled with a flammable liquid such as petroleum and supplied with a rag for a fuse that is lit just before being hurled, or filled with such a mix of flammable liquids that it ignites itself when it is smashed and its contents are exposed to air.
A city-state in Western Europe. Official name: Principality of Monaco.

It normally disappears three to five years after birth and almost always by puberty.

Morocco (a country in North Africa; official name: Kingdom of Morocco; capital: Rabat).

A brand of Chinese baijiu produced in the town of Maotai in the province of Guizhou.
A country in East Africa and Southern Africa. Official name: Republic of Mozambique (since 1990). Capital: Maputo.
An Iberian Christian living under Arab domination.
A continuum of closely related Romance dialects spoken in Muslim-dominated areas of the Iberian Peninsula during the early stages of Romance language development in Iberia.

(US, Canada) Abbreviation of mister. A title used before the surname in theory, though not generally in practice, above some undefined social level, too old to be addressed as “Master”, not a knight or of some higher rank, and, in Britain though not in the United States, not entitled to be addressed as “Dr.”.
a title used for a married couple before the surname or before the name of the husband.

Abbreviation of Missus or Mistress (used before an adult woman's name or surname, used for any high-status woman without regard to marital status until the 1800s, after which it began to be reserved for married, divorced and widowed women and used with their married surnames)
Title used before an adult woman's name or surname, especially when it is not desired or possible to indicate her marital status with Miss or Mrs.
A surname from German.
A person who has no magical abilities.
(Islam, uncountable) The figure who introduced Islam, and the man to whom the Qur'an was revealed; considered a prophet by Muslims and Baháʼís.

A megacity, the capital of Maharashtra, India, also known as Bombay.
The capital and largest city of Bavaria, Germany.
An autonomous community and province in southeast Spain.

An adage which states that if anything can go wrong, then it will.

Being or relating to a believer of Islam.
A person who is a follower and believer of Islam.
A en given name used by Muslims.

A country in Southeast Asia. Official name: Republic of the Union of Myanmar. Capital: Naypyidaw. Also known as Burma (which was formerly the official name).
An ancient Greek city in the NE Peloponnesus on the plain of Argos, inhabited since about 4000 B.C.E.

(topology) A one-sided surface formed by identifying two opposite edges of a square in opposite senses;a narrow strip given a half twist and joined at the ends, forming a three-dimensional embedding of said surface.
The capital city of Chad, located at the Chari river opposite Kousséri, Cameroon.
(logic) A binary operator composite of NOT AND; negation of AND function.

A en given name.

A town and commune in Aude department, Occitanie, southern France, formerly in the Languedoc-Roussillon region.

(Greek mythology) A youth who spurned the love of Echo and fell in love with his own reflection in a pool: in some versions of the myth, he drowned trying to reach it, while in others he sat fixated until a god took pity and transformed him into a flower.
A city and municipality of Estonia.
An American stock exchange based in New York City.
The capital city of the Bahamas.

A en given name borrowed from Russian in the twentieth century.
(biblical character) An Old Testament prophet who advised King David.
A en given name, of Biblical origin.

The ideology of the NSDAP (National Socialist German Workers' Party) in Germany, including an authoritarian government, ethnic nationalism (including but not limited to Pan-Germanism) and adequate territory (Lebensraum), and economic cooperation between the state and capital.
The ideology of any other (neo-)Nazi party; Nazism.
Nauruan, the language of Nauru.
the language of Nauru

An autonomous community and province in northern Spain.

It is an industrial and distribution center and major seaport located along the Mississippi near the Gulf of Mexico, known for its rich cultural heritage, especially its music and cuisine.

A native or resident of the state of New York in the United States of America.
A native or resident of New York City.

(mechanics) Newton's observation that to every action (force applied) there is an equal and opposite reaction (equal force applied in the opposite direction)

A en given name in continuous use since the 19th century.

(slang, derogatory, video games) A slavish supporter of Nintendo's video games or consoles; a Nintendo fanboy
Japanese
An island and country in Polynesia in Oceania, a self-governing state in free association with New Zealand. Official name: Republic of Niue. Capital: Alofi.

Any of the international prizes awarded annually by the Nobel Foundation for outstanding achievements in the fields of physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and for the promotion of world peace; or the prize in economics awarded by the Swedish National Bank, in memorial of Alfred Nobel.

(grammar) A noun case used in some languages to indicate movement away from something, removal, separation. In English grammar, it corresponds roughly to the use in English of prepositions "of", "from", "away from", and "concerning". In Latin grammar, the ablative case (cāsus ablātīvus) includes functions derived from the Indo-European ablative, instrumental, comitative, associative and locative cases; these cases express concepts similar to those of the English prepositions "of"/"from", "by", "with", "to"/"with", and "at"/"in", respectively. Here/hence/hither, there/thence/thither, and where/whence/whither are the only English words with separate forms for the ablative (motion away from) and lative (motion towards) cases.
